title: How Sam Parr vets business ideas: back-of-envelope math and a free research toolkit
summary: Sam argues ideas matter for people who actually ship, and that you vet them with quick back-of-envelope math plus lots of cheap research, not spreadsheets. He shares his research stack (Companies House, SimilarWeb, annual reports, Web Archive), how he cold-emails mentors, and why fear makes companies boring.

principles.text: Ideas matter for people who actually ship; if you only talk, send the link when it's live.
principles.quote: if you do have the skill of doing, which I would say all three of us have that I, I think ideas do matter because if you are trying to build something that grows quickly, you don't wanna put yourself down the wrong path.

principles.text: Vet ideas with back-of-envelope math. Detailed spreadsheet modeling early is fear-driven procrastination.
principles.quote: you just need back of the envelope math.

principles.text: Check a big player already exists in the market to confirm the idea is physically big enough, then add your own flavor.
principles.quote: I look at like, well who else out there is in the market? Well, how big are they? Oh, they're a billion dollars in revenue? Okay, I know that it's physically possible that this is a big enough idea.

principles.text: Research constantly with free tools like Companies House, SimilarWeb, annual reports and Web Archive to see how businesses really work.
principles.quote: I use annualreports.com, I use Similar Web, and I use Company's House.

principles.text: Test demand cheaply before building: a tiny version plus a few hundred dollars of ads can validate a business.
principles.quote: I spent $500 promoting the story and at the bottom of the website it said pay $5 a month to get part two

principles.text: Don't operationalize a new initiative too early; pilot small so people feel free to take risks and be weird.
principles.quote: I think a lot of times people, companies do boring stuff is because they're trying to operationalize things too much too early.
